events.summary: 8-K formally records that Snowflake CLOSED (on 2026-10-01) its private sale of $3.75 billion of 0.00% convertible senior notes: $2.0 billion due 2029 (conversion price about $500.38 per share) and $1.75 billion due 2031 (about $483.98 per share). Buyers have 13 days to buy up to $300 million more 2029 notes and $250 million more 2031 notes. Snowflake bought 'capped calls' (a hedge) with a cap of $820.30 per share, 150% above the reference price, costing about $383.5 million; about $548.3 million goes to repurchasing part of its 2027 convertible notes (about $261.8 million principal per the pricing release); the rest of the about $3.70 billion net proceeds is for general corporate purposes, including possible share buybacks and acquisitions. Maximum shares issuable on conversion: 7,009,480 (2029) plus 6,095,200 (2031). The deal itself was announced 2026-09-28 and priced that evening, so the closing is new paperwork, not new information.
events.why_it_matters: Zero-interest borrowing gives Snowflake about $3.7 billion of extra cash (versus about $4.3 billion of cash and investments at 2026-07-31 per the 10-Q). The cost to shareholders is possible dilution if the stock rises above about $484-$500 by maturity. Calculation (inference, high): at the initial conversion rates the notes convert into about 7.6 million shares (2,000,000 x 1.9985 + 1,750,000 x 2.0662), about 2.2% of the 352.8 million shares outstanding on 2026-08-21; the 8-K's maximum of about 13.1 million shares (about 3.7%) applies only in special cases. The capped call offsets dilution up to $820.30. Rules check: 8-K Item 3.02 matches the wording of a thesis breaker, but this is debt that converts into shares only if the price rises about 48-53%, not a share sale today.

products.name: 0.00% Convertible Senior Notes due 2029 and 2031 ($3.75 billion)
products.what_it_is: An IOU sold to big investors. It pays no interest, and the holder can swap it for Snowflake shares at about $484-$500 each.
products.analogy: A loan where the lender accepts no interest in exchange for the right to take shares instead of cash if the stock rises a lot.
products.buyers: Qualified institutional buyers (Rule 144A private placement), usually hedge funds running convertible-arbitrage strategies.
products.how_it_works: If SNOW stays below the conversion price, Snowflake repays the cash at maturity (2029/2031). If it rises above, holders convert and new shares may be issued. The capped call hedge offsets that dilution up to $820.30 per share.
products.price: Interest 0.00%. Conversion price about $500.38 (2029) and about $483.98 (2031), 52.5% and 47.5% premiums.
products.sales: $3.75 billion principal sold; about $3.70 billion net proceeds; option for up to $550 million more.
products.stage: Closed 2026-10-01; option to buy more open for 13 days.
products.size_for_company: Comparable to the company's roughly $4.3 billion of cash and investments at 2026-07-31. At initial rates it converts into about 2.2% of shares outstanding (inference, high).
products.why_investors_care: Cheap money for buybacks or acquisitions, against possible future dilution and a short-term price dip as convertible buyers hedge by shorting the stock (inference, medium).
products.watch_next: Whether the extra notes option is exercised (by about 2026-10-14), any buyback or acquisition funded with the cash, and diluted share count in the Q3 10-Q.

products.name: CoCo (AI coding agent) and CoWork (agentic workflow tool)
products.what_it_is: AI assistants built into Snowflake. CoCo writes and migrates data code; CoWork lets AI agents carry out tasks on a company's governed data.
products.analogy: CoCo is a junior programmer who knows your company's data warehouse; CoWork is an assistant allowed to act on that data within set permissions.
products.buyers: Data engineers and analytics teams at Snowflake's enterprise customers.
products.how_it_works: Customers run the agents inside Snowflake. Using them consumes computing credits, which Snowflake bills as product revenue (inference, medium; Futurum describes AI as a consumption driver, not a separate product line).
products.sales: Revenue not disclosed. Proxy: CoCo 9,100+ accounts (2,000+ added in Q2); CoWork 5,800 accounts. Management says AI products drove about half of Q2's growth acceleration.
products.size_for_company: Not disclosed separately; AI revenue run-rate not disclosed.
products.competition: Databricks and the cloud providers' own data and AI tools (AWS, Microsoft, Google), which are also Snowflake's infrastructure suppliers (10-Q risk factors). Competitor detail not sourced in this window.
products.why_investors_care: Evidence that AI adds to Snowflake's usage rather than replacing it. This is the core of the 2026 rebound and thesis point 2.
products.watch_next: Account counts and any AI revenue figure at Q3 results (expected 2026-12-02).

products.name: AWS infrastructure commitment ($6 billion over 5 years)
products.what_it_is: Snowflake's promise to buy at least $6 billion of Amazon cloud computing (including Graviton chips and GPU capacity) over five years.
products.analogy: A restaurant signing a 5-year bulk deal with its main food supplier: lower prices, but it must buy that much.
products.buyers: Snowflake is the buyer; AWS is the seller.
products.how_it_works: Snowflake runs on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. A large commitment usually buys better pricing, but Snowflake pays the shortfall if usage falls short (10-Q describes minimum-commitment risk).
products.price: $6 billion over five years (about $1.2 billion a year on average; inference)
products.sales: not applicable (this is a cost commitment, not a sale)
products.size_for_company: About 20% of FY27 product revenue guidance of $6.07 billion per year on average (inference).
products.why_investors_care: Signals management expects much more usage; affects gross margins.
products.watch_next: Gross margin trend in Q3 results.
